utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will see that we're again without Judge Chowhan. He is again unwell. He hopes to be back tomorrow. I have just spoken to him and he doesn't sound to me as though he will be back tomorrow; however, we have discussed the position before coming in and decided to continue on the same basis as we did yesterday. If anyone were to feel that they might be in any way prejudiced by that, we would expect them to draw it to our attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In a moment the cross-examination by Mr. Ackerman will continue. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration to speak the truth which you made at the beginning of your evidence will continue to apply to your evidence today. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely understand, Your Honour, but can we just pull the monitor closer to me in order to avoid further problems with my eyesight. My apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and good afternoon, General. Yesterday we talked a bit about where you were and what you were doing at various times in 1998 and I was looking at the transcript today, and I don't think that was very clear. So I would like to clarify that because it's important before we begin. I'd like you to just very methodically tell us between May and October of 1998, did you -- did you hold the same position between May and October of 1998?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout 1998 I held the same position, Chief of Staff and also deputy commander of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And during that period between May and October, could you tell us the times that you were actually in Kosovo and for how long each time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that I made several visits to Kosovo and Metohija throughout that time, but the only periods, I underlined for Your Honours' benefit, were the three that were lengthier, one between the 29th of May and the 8th of June. I spent part of this period at the forward command post of the Pristina Corps in Djakovica and another part at the Pec barracks. The other lengthier stay was between the 27th of July and the 28th of August that same year, when I established a forward command post for the 3rd Army in the Pristina barracks. The third period was between the 1st and the 10th of December, 1998, I spent this time at the Pristina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. I think that makes it very clear now. I'd like you to look at a document, it's 4D129, please. This is a regular combat report of the 3rd Army command dated 20 June 1998. The main reason I want you to look at this is more for form rather than substance, I guess. First of all, could you just tell the Judges what is a regular combat report and how often is it submitted and by whom and what kind of information should it contain?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that among other documents there were also combat reports being submitted by subordinate commands to the Supreme Command Staff. These combat reports by subordinate units were submitted up the chain of command to the highest level. These contained any activity taken during a particular day in the area of responsibility of whichever unit was submitting the combat report. In this case it was submitted by the 3rd Army command to the Supreme Command Staff. This is a combat report, and what this means is that there were combat operations afoot. In peacetime this would normally be termed an operations report. It is quite a formal document. It has a certain content, item by item. You can see it all for yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I'd like you to look at paragraph 5 of this document now --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's page 2 in the English and I think the same page in the B/C/S. We're just at paragraph 3 on the B/C/S. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There it is.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That paragraph is headed: "I have decided." Now, this is a report that is going from the 3rd Army up to the General Staff rather than an order going down from the 3rd Army to the Pristina Corps, I take it. Why does it contain this language: "I have decided"? Why is he telling the General Staff that he has decided something?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A report implies that a subordinate officer informs a superior officer. If you look at item 5 of this report, this reports on any activities taken that day in a formal way. It talks about the places of combat operations and who was conducting them. A subordinate commander informs his superior about his decision or - to put it in a different way - his intention in terms of what he would be doing the next day and how he would be using his own subordinate units. In the VJ we refer to that sort of document as decision, and that is why he is here using the term "I have decided." If I may just add something. When a superior officer receives such a report, if he agrees with the kind of decision that is taken and the way in which the units are to be used, the subordinate units, he may grant his approval. If he disagrees, he can challenge the decision, cancel the decision altogether, or abolish it, refute it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So then in the normal course of business the General Staff and General Perisic would have -- would have seen this document and would have made a decision as to whether or not to -- to approve that language "I have decided" language under paragraph 5; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. He doesn't need to write this up, his approval I mean. But if he disapproves, he must explain this in writing, what exactly he does not approve of, what exactly his orders now are, and what is to be changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the next paragraph, 5.1, which -- yeah, you can see it. Up above you have "I have decided." In this one it's called a "proposal of decision." What is the difference between "I have decided" and "proposal of decision"?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a part of the decision where he puts forward exactly what he means. In this part he proposes a specific deployment for the units, and then he gives the reasoning behind this decision. He also describes how he intends to go about implementing this, and that's why it is termed a proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I want to look at another document now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you do. Does that mean that it's the same as the previous one and he can act without approval and the only role that his superior, the Chief of the General Staff, has is if he disapproves of any of the action proposed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. The document I want to look at now is 4D297, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 4D297 is an order issued by General Pavkovic on 6 June of 1998, and he describes it as an order to prevent the illegal crossing from Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to the Republic of Albania. He points out there in the preamble that according to available information mass crossing of inhabitants of the Albanian ethnic minority from territories of Decani, Djakovica, and Prizren municipalities to the Republic of Albania is expected. And then he says that that act is aimed at showing the international community and the world public the exodus that is allegedly being done to them, so as provide a reaction of the international community. He says: "In order to prevent the mass crossing of citizens from the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to the Republic of Albania, I hereby order," and then you see his order in paragraph 1. And paragraph 1 is not completely showing on the screen in front of you, I realise that. Maybe we can scroll down and pick it up. It appears that what General Pavkovic is trying to do is prevent the exodus of Albanian civilians from Kosovo into the Republic of Albania; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I don't quite understand your question. Exodus, who exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, he's talking about the Albanian civilians, the -- going into the Republic of Albania, and it looks to me like in paragraph 1 he's trying to set up a system that will keep that from happening. I just wonder if you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may put it that way, yes, I entirely agree; but if I may, I would like to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You may explain.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had information that the terrorist army of Kosovo in addition to certain terror actions against the army and non-Albanians in general were carrying out this sort of operation also against their own ethnic fellows who weren't in favour of their ideas as well as against the rest of the population. And this was part of their media campaign that was supposed to benefit them. In order to prevent this, the corps commander here orders that should that be the case our units should do this or that, with a view to preventing this. If this fails he says how this should be secured, since in the previous period of time we had almost entirely blocked the border belt leaving open only certain parts that could still be taken; however, only our own men were aware of those that were still open.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do I rightly understand you to be saying, therefore, that these were genuine refugees driven out by their own countrymen who were terrorists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a combination of a number of different factors. It is natural that the population residing in an area where combat activities are afoot should try and flee to a safer area, that's one thing. On the other hand, there was pressure being exerted by the terror groups on these people, pressure on them to move out of the area so that this might then be used for propaganda purposes. And if I may, ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm satisfied with the answer you've given. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd finally like you to look down at the bottom of this document now, paragraph 5 and the paragraph immediately above it --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That would be the next page in B/C/S and in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Here General Pavkovic is talking about how this order is to be carried out. You'll see right above paragraph 5 he says: "Use force only in self-defence and to protect troops and combat equipment. The whole operation must be taped on video." And then in paragraph 5 he talks about: "If fire is opened on Yugoslav Army soldiers that they are to return fire, taking care not to fire at women, children, elderly, or other persons who are not shooting, but only on identified attackers. If this is not possible and would threaten the safety of civilians, find a way to disarm the attacker without using fire-arms." It appears here that General Pavkovic is going maybe almost above and beyond to try to protect those people from any kind of harm. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would use the phrase trying too hard. Even he's sacrificing his own people at the altar of the terrorists. What was he even saying here, if we cannot be certain by opening fire we will be successful in eliminating terrorists, in that case we should not fire at all. We should use other methods in order to stand in their way. Meanwhile his own units might sustain more than a handful of casualties. That is why I'm saying he even tried too hard, he invested too much into this particular effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I have another document for you to look at it's 4D134. This is a 3rd Army command order of 6 July 1998 to take up a forward command post for the 3rd Army in Pristina. And when we're talking about your time in Kosovo a few moments ago, you talked about being in this forward command post and being in Pristina for an extended period of time right around this time. I assume by that that you were actually part of the group that set up and occupied this forward command post for the 3rd Army at that point?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will now use military language. I was commander of a forward command post, I headed this group, having received authorisation from the army commander. And there is a written document to this effect where he bestows upon me the power to exercise command over the Pristina Corps, the command of the Pristina Military District, the 202nd military base, and the 211th Tactical Group. I had the power to make decisions, but my decisions were subject to verification by the army commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Why would General Samardzic -- well, we're going to have an answer to that. He indicates that it's based on his assessment of the security situation there, but can you give us more detail. Why would he want to set up a 3rd Army forward command post within the zone of responsibility of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I testified that the forward command post was set up wherever the focus of combat operations lay, the objective being to take in the situation in the area as quickly as possible, also bearing in mind the degree of my own authority. This made it possible for me to take decisions more swiftly and to react to certain situations that were arising. So that is why he set this up and that is why he endowed me with these powers. He wanted to curtail the time that the communication between the Pristina Corps on the one hand, the army, and feedback would take before measures were taken and such-like. In this way everything could be done on the spot in direct contact with the corps commander. Measures could be taken in keeping with any powers that we or they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This -- this I take it then basically has the effect of speeding up the normal chain of command so that -- that from the field all the way up to General Perisic one could keep closer touch of what was happening in the field in Kosovo; is that true?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, except I wouldn't say to speed up the chain. I would say to speed up the information flow within the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If I'd said it right, that's what I would have said, General. That's certainly what I meant. Now I want to look --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, why did it take until the 27th of July to establish -- to implement this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is the first order that we're looking at this. This is a preparatory order. You see that I used my group and put them at combat-readiness by a certain deadline and then the orders specifies a certain deadline for combat-readiness and for me to organise this command post and the deadline says within a seven-hour period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't follow that. The forward command post was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when the army commander decided to set up the command post, he issued an order for the command post group to prepare and he set a certain deadline, in this case the deadline was within seven hours, for them to turn up at their forward command post and be ready to continue their work. And that is why this amount of time elapsed between the order that constituted a preparation and the execution of the order itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When did the command post actually begin to function, the 3rd Army forward command post?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command post began to function on the 27th at 1500 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That was the Judge's question. Why did it take from the 6th of July until the 27th, 21 days, for that command post to get set up and functioning?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I'm not being sufficiently clear. An order to start preparations can be issued a month or two ahead of the order to execute. When this order will eventually be executed depends on what the situation in a certain area in which a commander is setting up a forward command post and getting it up and running. At one point in time, he believed that it was a good time to start this, so he did and he was perfectly within his right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I want to go now to another document, it's 4D91, and we're going to spend a bit of time with this document, I think it's a particularly interesting document. This document is dated 30 July 1998, and this is after that forward command post had started to function and it's an order from General Samardzic. And if you look at the preamble to that, does that indicate that this order is issued pursuant to an order that he had received from the commanding general, the Chief of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A forward command post can be established pursuant to an order from the commander or the superior. At -- in this case both orders existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But he seems to be saying in that preamble that the order he's issuing here is pursuant to an order from the Chief of the General Staff. Is that what that's saying there or am I misreading it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're reading it correctly. And if the interpretation was correct, I think my answer was correct too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. The first paragraph of that order speaks about you. It says: "The Chief of Staff shall control the work and organisation of work of [sic] the Army forward command post in Pristina," correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there a problem with the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Apparently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you not hear that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm having a problem with the question because that's not what it says here. It says here that I will organise the work of the command post not of the army in Pristina. Organise work and work at the forward command post in the Kosovski Junaci barracks in Pristina, so that's only the work of the forward command post. It doesn't refer to the barracks or the soldiers in the barracks. They have their own commander, although he was subordinate to me but in a different way, under a different paragraph in this order, as you'll see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, paragraph 2 seems to provide that: "Decisions concerning the engagement of army forces and reinforcement in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija shall be made by" you in line with decisions issued by General Samardzic, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as I explained previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 3 he talks about meetings of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija. He says that: "The commander of the Pristina Corps," which is General Pavkovic, before he goes to one of those meetings needs to meet with you or acquaint you in some way with any requests that he's aware of. He's supposedly explained to you the proposals for the engagement of forces with reinforcements, and then after your consent he goes to the meeting. Then after the meeting, he comes back to you and reports to you on proposals that had been accepted or any other requests which diverge from the proposal that he told you about earlier and requests permission relating to those requests. If he gets that permission from you or he takes your decision at least and then informs the Joint Command of what decisions you have made. Is that a fair reading of that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, fully. But it would be necessary to explain the methodology of work, if you will allow me and if there is enough time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is enough time, and I think that it's important that there be some explanation about this. It appears that clearly the army through General Samardzic and you, are keeping complete control of their own forces and not being directed in any way by the Joint Command but simply deciding on whether or not to accept proposals from that group. Is that a fair analysis of what this paragraph is talking about?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked you if I can explain the methodology, and in your question that's partly so. Will you allow me to explain the methodology and it will be much clearer? The corps commander, my subordinate whose competency of commander was transferred to the Chief of Staff were duty-bound according to the plan of work of the forward command post to be at the command post, forward command post, at 1830 in the operations room, where they would report on the activities of their subordinate units in the course of the day, explain their ideas for the engagement of the units on the following day, and once they had done that I would approve or alter or challenge, deny. And with such an approved, amended, or denied decisions, the corps commander as a member of the Joint Command would go to the meeting. And there they would analyse these things, and if they had any requests which were considerably different from the decision I had approved, they would have to ask for approval for it. If not, then he would act upon the decision that had been approved. If he asked for an amendment, I would have to say either yes or no and then he would have to refer back to the Joint Command and he would have to inform them of what I had said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So is it fair to say that that Joint Command nor anybody in that Joint Command could direct General Pavkovic or you to engage VJ forces in any way, that that was up to you to decide that along with General Samardzic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. The commander of the army and I through the normal chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I want to look now at a document 4D378. This is a very small and simple document. It's signed I think by you dated 31 July 1998. And in paragraph 1 of that document which is called an order, you order that: "On 3 August 1998 use some of the Pristina Corps troops to rout and destroy terrorist forces in the Smonica village sector, establishing full control of the sector, and ensuring safe use of the Djakovica-Batusa road." Now, that I think comports with what you've been telling us, that when you took over as Chief of Staff there at the 3rd Army forward command post you basically became the commander in Pristina Corps at that point and could issue orders like this that would then be carried out by General Pavkovic and the Pristina Corps, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is partly correct if the interpretation is correct, you said that I practically became the commander of the Pristina Corps. No. I was only the superior of the commander of the Pristina Corps. I issued a task to him, not to his units which would execute the task, and that is a major and significant difference. Because in that case if it were so, the commander of the Pristina Corps would have been replaced in the chain of command. If your question was correctly interpreted, then that would have meant -- been what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, that paragraph that we're referring to there refers to terrorist forces in the Smonica village sector. Is that area inside the border belt or outside the border belt?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is dated the 31st of July. Extending the border belt to 5 kilometres, that was done on the 21st of July if I remember correctly. And Smonica was not within the border belt but it was on the road and it was threatening supplies to the units at the border posts, which is why in order to make sure the road was passable, we had to break up and rout to this terrorist group which was preventing the supply columns going to Morina and Kosare border posts. This is on the Djakovica-Ponosevac road, some 10 kilometres away from Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was General Perisic or the General Staff regularly informed regarding the engagement of VJ units in Kosovo? Were there daily combat reports going up to them regarding these activities?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you recall ever receiving any orders from General Perisic or communications from him expressing disagreement with activities like the one we're -- that's showing here on the screen? Did he ever express his concerns that you might have been acting illegally or something?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to me personally, but I have to distance myself from this. I don't know what the relations were between my commander and the Chief of the General Staff. I know what the relations were between my commander and myself as the Chief of Staff. My commander never denied any decisions that I approved or challenge any decisions that I approved during the time that I was there. He never concluded that the army was used beyond the scope of the orders of the competent superior officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. To continue this concept let's look at 4D141, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, on page 16, lines 14, or rather, 15 and 16, the witness said: "I know what the relations were like between myself and my commander." This might refer to the Chief of Staff. He said he did not know about the relations between the commander and the Chief of Staff and that he did know about the relations between himself and his commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the sense of that is quite clear as it stands, but thank you anyway for endeavouring to clarify it. Please continue, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 4D141 is another regular combat report coming from the 3rd Army forward command post, actually, up to the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army. And this is the kind of report we were just referring to where the activities going on there in Kosovo were being reported up through the chain to the General Staff and presumably to General Perisic. I'd like you to look at section 3 of this document "situation in army units in Kosovo and Metohija."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I think that can be found on page 2 of both documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, what's being reported there in paragraph 3 is this: "Part of the army forces supported MUP forces around 1000 hours they were engaged in routing terrorist forces in the sector of the villages of Gramocelj, Prilep, and Glodjane" and reached the line Gornji Bites village and fighting is going on in Prilep village. And it talks about an axis Porobica village, Krst Rokoc and Rastovica village axis. These areas are they -- they're also outside the border belt, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not completely. Some of the villages are within the 5-kilometre border belt and some are outside it, beyond it, but along the roads. For example, Prilep is on the Djakovica-Decani road.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: After this document was submitted to the General Staff, was there any negative reaction that you were aware of from General Perisic regarding the portion of these operations that were outside the border belt?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I take it if General Perisic had wanted to, he could have very easily issued an order to the 3rd Army and the Pristina Corps not to conduct any operations outside the border belt, couldn't he?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. Each one of our commands to the army command, through the operations centres had protected channels where by pressing a certain button you could get through to every command and convey an order, yes, no, do this, stop that, and so on, so he could have done that momentarily as soon as he read the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I take it you never saw or heard of an order from General Perisic to the army not to operate outside the border belt during this period?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He ordered that the border be secured, that the units in the area be secured, and that supplies to the units be enabled. That was enough for us soldiers to understand what this means. If the road has been cut off in the Smonica area and my supply convoy cannot take supplies to the border posts, I have to take certain combat action in order to carry out the task. And he was aware when he issued this order what it meant. He knew what the content of the order was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And with this report that we saw just now in paragraph 3 he also was aware that the army was involved in supporting the MUP forces in some of these kind of engagements, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to look now at 4D229.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yesterday I use the term "inspection" to describe something the General Staff was doing in Kosovo and there was a -- an error in translation so that it was a tour or a visit not an inspection. The English here says that what this is ordering is an investigation team to come to Pristina. This is an order from General Perisic ordering this investigation team to come to Pristina and carry out certain tasks which are set out there in paragraph 2. Were you familiar with this order and what happened with regard to it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Of course I'm familiar with it. The Chief of the General Staff by this order is sending an investigation team - I apologise to the lawyers - not to carry out investigations of crimes but an investigation team which was supposed to study the method of working, see the positive and negative experiences, because these are for all teachers in a high military schools, people who teach tactics, strategy, and so on, so that later on we could transform this into textbooks for our schools. That's why he set up an investigation team.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. If you look at -- this is 30 July of 1998 where -- right there near the end of July right after your forward command post began to operate. If you look at paragraph 2 one of the tasks he assigns to this group is to propose an engagement of Yugoslav Army commands and units in anti-terrorist actions in the Pristina Corps zone of responsibility, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer because I don't see this document on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's paragraph 2, the second part of paragraph 2 right there, it's being highlighted for you.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This same document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that in my previous response I've already said that this investigation team was supposed to look at the way units were used and how they were operating in an anti-terrorist operation, in fighting the terrorist army of Kosovo, and to extract all the positive and negative experiences.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, is there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I think you should get the witness to read the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you need to read the second paragraph. I think there may be a translation problem. So just read it very carefully and let the people in the booth translate it and let's see what it actually says.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Task of the team: Analysis of the state of organisation, functioning, and prospects of development of terrorist actions and proposal of the engagement of the commands and units of the Army of Yugoslavia in anti-terrorist activities in the area of responsibility of the Pristina Corps."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, so what I'm asking you is: Was he asking them to propose to him some plan for engagement of the army against the terrorists, or is that a misreading of this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that is so. This investigating team had no competence to propose how the corps should be used in anti-terrorist operations. That was the exclusive right of the corps commander and the army commander, to propose how the forces would be used. This team was established for scholarly purposes, simply to work out a methodology for arriving at results which might later on be used to establish standards and normative documents. They were to study the use, but they had nothing to do with the current use of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. I think you've made that very clear now and I appreciate you clarifying it. I want to go now to the document 4D375, and this is another General Pavkovic order of 18 August 1998. And it's characterised as an order for the prevention of theft and procedure with stolen equipment. And I'm primarily interested, in general, in that first paragraph. General Pavkovic says: "Despite a number of written orders which have been issued in the strictest terms, the looting of houses and places where Albanian terrorists stayed or in the zones and sectors where the Pristina Corps units were deployed has apparently gone on, recently been observed. He says this discredits the army and its role in society in the greatest of fashions, hampering efforts to calm the situation, and initiating attempts by certain structures and organisations to accuse the army of organised looting. And then he enters some orders regarding the prevention of looting. My question really is this: It seems that General Pavkovic was having some difficulty controlling the looting among the lower echelons of the Pristina Corps. Do you have any idea why that would have been a difficult thing to control and why he was having this problem?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the explanation is quite simple. There was a large number of men in a certain area. Each person reacts differently to various stressful situations. In this case activity by the terrorist army of Kosovo. There are people who are prone to theft, getting drunk, looting, and so on, and he says in the preamble that such things had happened. And now he wants, based on this information, to acquaint the entire corps once again that all measures should be taken to prevent such phenomena and that criminal proceedings should be instituted against the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And apparently this was going on in spite of orders that he had issued previously, saying that it would be heavily prosecuted and it's illegal to loot, it still continued to go on. So I guess it was difficult to control, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you one thing. We commanders are in charge of exercising control, and he was showing his concern from the point of view of his responsibility for this kind of thing and that's why he's issuing this order. Even today in peacetime we have normatively regulated relations, and still there is excessive behaviour, looting, murder, and so on. That happens everywhere, let alone in a war situation. That's why because of this high degree of responsibility he thought it was necessary once again to point out that problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. The next document and almost the last one is 3D697. This is a document dated 2nd October 1998 from the 3rd Army forward command post titled: "Analysis of the tasks executed on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija." First of all, do you know who prepared this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know who drafted it, and if you scroll this up you will see that it was done by an officer from the command post, from the group that is at the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And to whom was this directed? Who was this supposed to be sent to? Who was this for?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At a forward command post we always have an operations centre that functions, and there is work there round the clock 24 hours a day, in shifts. When this analysis was carried out, since from the operations centre where all this information is later entered into the war diary, no one could be present because one shift was resting, the other one was working. Then an officer was engaged from the command post, if I'm not mistaken it was Colonel Vasovic, I think; and on my orders, since I attended that meeting, too, or rather, this analysis, he kept the minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What I'm having trouble understanding is: For whose eyes was this written? I mean, who was supposed to receive this analysis?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This analysis is used within the command post and it is entered into the war diary. This is a temporary document. I was supposed to verify it, but I verified it through the war diary because the person signing the war diary was not at the meeting concerned. Had that person been there, then on the basis of this temporary document, this analysis, this person would have entered this into the war diary and signed the war diary for that day. It was only used by him as an auxiliary thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. If we look then at paragraph 1.1 where it talks about definition of tasks, the last bullet point I guess we call it there is: "Provide support to the MUP forces in dispersing and destroying KLA forces in accordance with your requirements and abilities, making sure not to disrupt the level of combat-readiness required by the commands and the units for the execution of basic tasks." I don't quite understand that. It says: "In accordance with your requirements and abilities." Whose requirements and abilities are being talked about there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I wasn't clear a few moments ago when I explained. This is an analysis of a certain period at the forward command post --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, you just need to tell us whose requirements and abilities you understand to be being referred to there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Requirements and needs of the MUP and our abilities, our possibilities, whether we can help in terms of these requirements of the MUP so that we do not endanger the implementation of our main task securing the state border, and of course communications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And these tasks that are defined here, it says these are pursuant to the order of the Chief of the General Staff and then a number of other orders. I assume that sets out the source for the definition of these tasks; is that true?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know where the war diary is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The war diary is in the archives of every unit, in the archives of the Army of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The archives of the Army of Serbia are in Belgrade. That is where all these documents were obtained from, through the National Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where in Belgrade are the war diaries kept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I cannot give you the exact street and number because I really don't know, but there are these military archives where all documentation from that wartime period is stored.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your explanation for the analysis being done by Vasovic seemed rather odd to me. If there is a person who is responsible for keeping the war diary, why on earth did you not get him to do the analysis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I tried to explain. Our duty shifts in the operation centre --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your explanation meant that the exercise had to be done twice. Vasovic had to do it and then you had to go through the war diary and check it. Why did you not just wait until who --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- The -- why did you not just wait until whoever did the -- kept the diary came back on duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not understand your question. At the operations centre there are persons who are on duty non-stop at the communications centre and also entering certain information on the map. Part of the personnel are resting, that would be the next shift, that is why no one was there. And I as the most responsible person in addition to the commander attended that meeting. This Vasovic was engaged to do that, whereas later I was supposed to check the accuracy of this information, whether it was correctly entered and whether it was correctly entered in the war diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, sorry, I remain completely puzzled on this. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: General, we're going to leave this document. We're going to look now at a document -- well, I have some questions to ask you before we look at another document. When did General Samardzic leave the command of the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the exact date. I think it was right after the new year, in the month of January 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know what his next assignment was?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because -- his next assignment was precisely what we did not understand each other about yesterday, that was the head of the inspectorate of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the transcript line 19 says January 2000. I think the witness said January 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness said 2000.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there you are, Mr. Ackerman, another one to clear up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if General Pavkovic took over the 3rd Army in December of 1999, General Samardzic must have left about that time.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you that I left before Commander Samardzic left. The exact date and when the handover exactly took place, on which date, I cannot say, but as far as I remember it was the beginning of January 2000. I cannot define this specifically because I had already gone to the Federal Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When was the war, the NATO bombing, when was that, what year was that? That was 1999, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1999, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the commander of the 3rd Army during that period of time was General Pavkovic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I'm a bit confused, am I not. I do apologise to the Trial Chamber. It was a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I'm glad we got that cleared up.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war, General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were you in the Ministry of Defence for the whole period from October until the 3rd of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not from October. In accordance with the ordinance I left my duty on the 31st of December, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in the ministry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. You've -- well, I take it you were in the ministry from then until you became the assistant Chief of General Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, and changing two duties at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The new assignment for General Samardzic, was that a demotion or a promotion?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In military hierarchy, that was promotion because it is customary that the chief inspector -- I mean before when we had the Yugoslav People's Army, this organ was called the Main Inspectorate of National Defence, Main Inspectorate of National Defence of the Army of Yugoslavia. Now it's the Main Inspectorate of the Army of Yugoslavia, so it is a higher rank than army commander because he can, with his team, come and exercise control over the commander of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. After he left, General Pavkovic took over. Did you know General Pavkovic well enough to give us your opinion regarding his capabilities as an officer in the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With your leave, I'd like to say I know him quite well. When I became Chief of Staff in 1996, he was in the operative organ of the Pristina Corps. Later on he left and then he came -- well, this is a very capable, educated, responsible officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at one final document, it's 4D136. Can you tell the Chamber what this is?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every officer in our army has an official assessment after a certain period of time or one that is done along fast tracks if he is being reassigned and so on. This is a official assessment of General Pavkovic. According to our methodology an official assessment is provided by the army commander, having consulted his closest associates. In terms of official assessment, this is the personnel department and the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Ackerman, please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, the draft assessment is discussed by the commander's collegium where all members of the collegium can exercise their influence and then it is for the commander to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we look at the last page of this document, apparently there's a sort of final assessment by General Samardzic of General Pavkovic. In English it says -- his assessment is positive with the mark exceptional. Is that a high assessment, medium, low? What is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Some question --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the very top. Excellent, "odlican," is the very top. For a student, a 10 is a top mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. That's all I have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, can you help us from your own point of view with one matter. Can you indicate the number of witnesses led by other parties that you envisage cross-examining in this way?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Probably not more than one or two more in my mind right now. This is a witness that it was kind of touch and go between the two of us whether he'd be my witness or Mr. Visnjic's witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And are the others in Mr. Visnjic's case?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Maybe one more, probably none more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It depends a little bit on the motion that I have pending that we discussed a little bit earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And later than that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know. Nothing that's in my mind right now. Can I get some sense of what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it must be obvious to you that there's a difference between cross-examination in the sense of defending yourself against what's coming from your co-accused and making your own case when it comes to our assessment of how you're using the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the division of that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's -- I think that in this Tribunal what we try to do is minimise inconvenience for witnesses; that's why we have joint trials so we don't have to bring a witness four times. The other choice I had of course would be to call this witness back in my own case. I think that's highly inefficient. And there are witnesses who can give evidence for more than one party here. I think this is a efficient way to go about it, but if you disagree I'll go the other way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's no disputing from that point of view it's efficient. But when you look at what we are trying to do in balancing the interests of everyone, including the Prosecution here and when you bear in mind the order we made about the time available to present the Defence case, we have to decide whether this is part of that time or whether this is ancillary cross-examination time for which further allowance has to be made because the parties are not necessarily the individual accused are not at one in relation to a particular witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it makes huge sense for you to see this as part of my time and presenting my case. That's a fairly obvious view to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've answered the point for me and thank you very much for doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all I would like to add something to what you've been discussing with Mr. Ackerman. Until now I fully support his point of view. I have about 15 questions and the question pertain specifically to some findings from the 98 bis ruling specifically related to my client, and I believe that the answers to these questions are going to resolve at least one witness from my list, he won't even have to come. So perhaps it looks like a waste of time now, but you will see ultimately we are saving a lot of time, the fact that we are cross-examining witnesses that could be called by us, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed. But that also simply confirms the point that Mr. Ackerman made at the end, that that really is effectively part of the time for the presentation of your case. And I'm grateful to you all for clarifying that because it makes our task in assessing the situation easier. So please continue, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Your Honour, then I have to know how much time I'm permitted for cross and how much time will be taken away from my own time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will be able to distinguish between questions that are dealing with challenges that witnesses led by other accused are making against you, which I suspect may be a bit later in the case, and the evidence you are leading which is clearly supporting a positive case. Now, I think the whole of Mr. Ackerman's cross-examination fell under the latter category. I appreciate the difficulty when it's mixed, and we may have to come to you and have a look at that and we'll do it informally and give you an opportunity to respond, and you know that you do get a record of the use of time that you can have a look at and come and speak to the legal staff or court staff and check on it. But I'm extremely grateful for the clarification because that enables us just to get our heads down and get on with it, subject to one other issue which I raised the other day with Mr. Visnjic. And we may have to address that one if there is no significant change in his line-up. So please continue, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just one more instruction before I start. Are we working in accordance with the same schedule that we had yesterday, until 4.00? When's the break? Are we working as we did yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, the break will be as able at quarter to, and if you want it now we'll come back at ten past.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, I don't want to disturb it in any way. I just needed to know when to break off. Please don't take that off my time, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Simic, or rather, General Simic. I am Mihajlo Bakrac and I represent General Lazarevic, who you probably know. So I'm going to start with my first question now in this respect. General, if I understood things correctly, towards the end of 1997/the beginning of 1998 you were Chief of Staff of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't understand it right. As for that duty I assumed it on the 7th of July, 1996, and I remained there until the end of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: That is to say the end of 1997/beginning of 1998 you held that position?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Perhaps we didn't understand each other. Do you know perhaps that at the end of 1997, or rather, at the beginning of 1998 General Lazarevic was Chief of Staff of the Nis Corps, also within the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, precisely he was my subordinate because I was Chief of Staff, and the 319th Regiment was the communications link for the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know and is it correct that by an order of the Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, General Perisic, Vladimir Lazarevic in the beginning of 1998 was transferred to be -- from the -- to be the Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps after having been in the Nis Corps?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But he couldn't have gone through any other order. There was just one other possibility; that is to say that if the president were to appoint him general through an ordinance, otherwise colonels fall within the remit of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, you explained about the formation of the forward command post of the 3rd Army in Pristina. Can you explain to me - and we have seen a document that says on the 20th an order was passed, and then if I understood things correctly, on the 21st --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 21st of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes. The forward command post of the Pristina Corps in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honour, in the transcript there is a mistake. My question was: Is it correct that on the 21st of the forward command post of the Pristina Corps in Djakovica was taken up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We have your answer but I'm just repeating my question for the purposes of the transcript. You explained to us that when the situation becomes more complex it becomes necessary to establish a forward command post. Can you explain to us why this forward command post in Djakovica was established or, perhaps even better, perhaps I can ask for 3D697, an analysis of the implementation of tasks in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have page 2 shown on our screens, paragraph 1, item 4, command of the forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, you see it on your screen on the right-hand side. 1.4, commanding the forces. Would you please be so kind as to read out loud the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean 1.4, commanding the forces?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I mean, the first sentence alone.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "For commanding the forces of the corps deployed along the state border and in the area a forward command post of the Pristina Corps in Djakovica was set up on the 21st of April, 1998."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that we see what the task was and when you say the situation was becoming more and more complex, can you tell us why the need to set up a forward command post for the Pristina Corps in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I provided a very comprehensive answer already when I spoke about the forward command post of the 3rd Army in this case. The need arose for the unit to be in closer proximity to where all this was going on, and this was the state border, the border belt where the terrorist forces were more and more and in more and more brazen way were bringing in weapons from Albania, thereby posing a threat to the local population. That is why the commander decided that he should have on the spot a commander who was in a position to take swift decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's time for our break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, we have to break at this stage for half an hour. Would you please leave the courtroom with the usher, and we shall resume at --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we shall resume at 4.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry for confusing the length of the two breaks, but you're still only getting 20 minutes at the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I've been trying to save time. I'm up on my feet, as you can see, waiting for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard the interpretation, so you can chock this down to my expense, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, sir, let us not repeat what I've asked you already and you've answered before the break. For the reasons that you mentioned in your answer, are you aware of the fact that General Lazarevic, then Colonel Lazarevic, all the time from the time he took up the forward command post in Djakovica and until the end of that year, 1998, stayed right there at the Djakovica forward command post?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, when you answer "yes," a short answer and then I make a pause, that's for the purposes of the interpretation, not because I'm expecting you to go on with your answer. Just to be clear on that. General, speaking of the forward command post, would you be so kind as to tell me what other kinds, what other types of command posts are envisaged in military doctrine?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In military theory there are several different types of command post: Basic command post, reserve command post, rear command post, false command post, forward command post, and joint command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, I want to know about the latter. What exactly does this mean, joint command post?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is often the case that in a certain area where combat operations are afoot, actions are being carried out by a number of different bodies that do not share a single chain of command. In order to unify all these different strands and in order to bring about some degree of coordination between these units to prevent conflict in the area, what one does is one sets up a joint command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, page 37, 17, the witness said different units and we see the interpretation here different bodies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said units belonging to different bodies or structures in terms of the chain of command, which means they do not share a single chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. Sir, the Djakovica forward command post, it had a direct contact with the Pristina Corps command, didn't it? It also had an encrypted telephone line connecting it to the command of the 3rd Army and a direct line to the operations centre of the main staff of the VJ; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that it had a contact. It was in terms of its chain of command that there was certain communication lines between this unit and its superior command. There was a possibility for them to get in touch directly with the General Staff of the VJ. In military terminology we don't use the word "contact"; we use the term chain of command, subordinate/superior/subordinate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. And excuse my lay language when it comes to military doctrine. I will try not to blunder like that again, sir, in order to speed things along. General, sir, you did tell us about that, I believe. Is it true that as Chief of Staff of the 3rd Army late in 1998 you headed an expert team of the VJ that produced a study concerning problems of securing the state border facing Macedonia and Albania, the then-Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps, Lazarevic, was also a member of that group, right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I remember I think that was in December when I said that between the 1st and the 10th of December I was there. So the answer to your question is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it true that the finding of the expert team indicated that one of the chief problems in terms of securing the state border was a lack of manpower or forces to actually get the state border secured, right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the overall conclusion. But if I may elaborate on this, when you have a border like that you never have enough power to fully secure it. We could have drafted as many men as we liked. We would never have been successful given the lie of the land and the depth of the border belt in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: As a consequence, nearly throughout 1998 there were many terrorist strikes from Albania against those securing the state border, and this resulted in -- frequently resulted in deaths, right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I have to correct you on this. The security organs working along the state border because the interpretation I got was different. The security organs, but these are the border belt security organs and we distinguish between these two.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it true that every time an incident like this occurred an attack being carried out against organs securing the state border the following measures were taken, informing by the border battalion to the Pristina Corps the 3rd Army and then all the way to the General Staff of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is a perfectly normal line of information or information flow, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it true that an on-site investigation was carried out by the relevant bodies of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If there were casualties or deaths on either side, that was exactly what would normally be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it true that in these cases an investigation would be carried out on the spot by a military investigative judge from Nis?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and the forensic team.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it true that in these cases a report would be submitted to a mixed interstate commission in order for an on-site investigation to be carried out to see what exactly had happened?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was the methodology used along all state borders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What about after the OSCE mission arrived, were such incidents regularly reported to the OSCE mission for verification?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In addition to pointing out the thing about the reporting in terms of the chain of command and the mixed state border commission, they too were informed so that they might be involved in the on-site investigation. And this information was forwarded to them through the appropriate bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And then charges would be pressed by the relevant bodies of the judiciary, right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if there was any misuse of somebody's official or professional capacity - and I mean those working along the state border and securing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. Is it also true that the command of the 3rd Army back in 1998 issued a number of orders regulating the use of units in combat assignments in keeping with the rules of combat?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Nearly -- there were several such orders. There were several such orders, although on the other hand theatrically speaking in terms of military theory, that would not have been required. That's what they teach at military schools. This is a superfluous statement to make in an order, but commanders felt responsible and they saw fit to repeat this likewise many times if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What about the command of the 3rd Army, did it not in certain situations restrict the use of units even in keeping with the rules of combat; and if so, why?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By all means. Initially when I was at the forward command post of the army there was the restriction that I would only allow large-calibre weapons to be used, the reason being I wanted to prevent the lower-ranked commanders from misusing their position, not so much that I wanted to keep them from using certain weapons inappropriate and not what a situation called for. For example, you have a terrorist and you target them with an artillery weapon which is just a very common place example of a possible mistake. So that is why we placed under control the weapons of large-calibre, and then later when the commander came and stepped in, when he took over the command post, he took over dealing with this sort of problem, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now call up 5D106.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're content that the transcript reflects that answer, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm just about to check. My colleague, Mr. Cepic, is also checking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, did you say that when you were at the forward command post you would only allow large-calibre weapons to be used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to be a little more accurate. When I was at the forward command post only large-calibre weapons were weapons that I was in charge of, and that was one of the tasks that I had and the reasons that I was at the forward command post of the Pristina Corps. Later on as the intensity of operations in the area increased, a decision was approved and a proposal was made by the corps commander in terms of what he wished to use. And by the same token, I allowed for these weapons to be used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please call up 5D106.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, just before you do that, I still am confused. Did you also say that you have a terrorist and you target them with an artillery weapon which is a commonplace example of a common mistake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think there is something wrong with the interpretation. I merely vulgarized a possible proposal, a possible example of something happening, but I said that when I was - and I repeat - at the forward command post of the Pristina Corps approved weapons of large calibres to be used. Later on when I was at the forward command post of the 3rd Army, through a proposal of a decision of the commander of the Pristina Corps, where you can see his notion and the engagement of forces with this -- his own equipment, then by approving the decision itself I approved the use of those weapons that he defined in his decision. There was no need - and let me emphasise this - you cannot use this mortar, this artillery weapon, and so on and so forth. He proposed whatever his idea was. If I approved a decision, then by default I also approved the use of those weapons. I'm not sure how clear I'm making this for you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may be the question -- I perhaps am having difficulty because I don't understand why the question was asked. But I understand you to be saying that large-calibre weapons were used against terrorists; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may clarify this. My question was this: Was this used restrictively and only when a need arose? Maybe it's my question that originally led to this slight confusion. And who gave the order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, restrictively, and I was the one who was given the right to make an assessment, in the belief that I was placed sufficiently high up in the army to decide what weapon would be used. And this reflects the restrictive nature of this and not some lack of trust on the part of the subordinates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Now we've got this clarified, General. Now we have 5D106 before us, and if you look at paragraph 2 of the order, this is an order by the army commander, Dusan Samardzic. It reads, first of all, that the army units based on his orders would be required to provide assistance to the MUP forces, and then paragraph 2, artillery of large calibre may only be used based on his approval. Does this prove what you just said?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this confirms what I just said a while ago. But let's try to avoid any misunderstanding. The date here is the 7th of August and the command post has already been set up, and I was the one who called the shots. However, when the commander was around, by his very presence he would annul anything that he had transferred to me previously and then he would take decisions. So that was the principle used.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Were there situations when limiting the use of weapons was done when the KLA were using civilians as a human shield or diplomatic representatives or foreign journalists if they were present?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an express prohibition for opening fire if there were civilians, children, women, elderly in front and the civilians were shooting from the crowd. I've already stated that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see in e-court Exhibit P969.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, you will see before you an order from the command of the Pristina Corps signed by the Chief of Staff, Colonel Lazarevic. If you can take a look at it, please, I think there's on error in the document. It's P969?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, that's the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Where it says: "I order," the first passage under that. "Before opening fire, unit commanders are to assess whether international observers are in the sector of combat disposition of Siptar terrorists, and if they are there do not open fire." Is this order in compliance with the order of the higher command, saying that fire must not be opened in the cases we have just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. Our main aim was to rout and destroy the terrorist army of Kosovo, not any civilians who may be around or any diplomatic representatives, as mentioned here. And I've already mentioned the population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Again, I'm not fully understanding this, Mr. Bakrac. Where's the reference to assessing whether civilians are involved or in the line?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the first paragraph above the order it says: "With the aim of preventing units from the corps of opening uncontrolled and unnecessary fire at Siptar terrorists, I hereby order ..." And then below it says: "Before opening fire unit commanders are to assess whether international observers are in the sector of combat disposition of Siptar terrorists and if they are thought to be there, do not open fire."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is the mistake you say there is in this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's not form of a telegram, and when it showed up on the screen I thought it wasn't the correct document; but later I established that it was. I think that it is in the transcript what I said that it is after all the document I asked for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
