utterances.text: But you do accept there's no reference to civilians here, other than international observers?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I was asking the General to explain the various cases in which there were restrictions to opening fire, and this is just one of the examples. And to save time, we weren't looking for other examples as well, we thought that one would suffice.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps I should ask the question at this stage also. Why not open fire when there are international observers present? That would suggest a different approach if they weren't present.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this can be interpreted in two different ways. As a soldier and as someone who is familiar with such document, the way I understand it is that regardless of the presence of the terrorists whom we wish to destroy, we should not open fire so that innocent people, and in the previous document the civilian population was mentioned, we should not open fire, regardless of the presence or the shooting of the terrorists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, is that what the previous document said?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, I think the General was thinking of the documents shown to him by Mr. Ackerman previously. I didn't want to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were similar questions before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did the other document say if there were civilians present, do not open fire? That's not my recollection of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I said. We saw an order here and I even said that the commander sacrificed his own units. If there were terrorists among a crowd of civilians and they were opening fire, they should be liquidated if possible; but if not possible, then other ways must be found to do it. I said that yesterday when asked about a document by counsel for General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's document 4D297, paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we have that on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, do you remember and do you agree with me that in August 1998 one of the strongest strongholds of the KLA armed rebellion was the area of Junik and the surrounding villages and do you know what villages these are?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely yes, starting from Djakovica, Smonica, Jasic, Junik, Slup, Decani, Voksa, Prilep. I can't enumerate all the villages now, but it's on the stretch from Djakovica to Decani. There's a main road and then there's another road going over Junik which is closer to the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that there was an assessment that the KLA forces numbered over a thousand terrorists in that area?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the approximate number. No one can confirm whether that's the precise number or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The command of the 3rd Army, General, in daily combat reports always included a special point concerning the engagement of the Pristina Corps units at the forward command post up to the level of combat group, and it reported on this to the staff. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, certainly, that was their duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have on e-court Exhibit 5D1174. Your Honour, this is one of two documents, and I have only four or five more, which I would like to have the witness comment on. But they have not been translated yet, so I move that they be marked for identification and I will comment only on a few brief sentences with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, this is a continuing problem. I have no objection proceeding this way and I'll deal with it as necessary. I may make a request further on depending on what it shows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. They will be marked for identification. Please continue, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise to my learned friend, Mr. Hannis. We uploaded it into the system and sent it for translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, you have before you on the screen a regular combat report. I apologise, but to clarify to you and the Court, simply for the sake of speeding up the proceedings and saving time, I will read and you will only confirm whether what I read is correct or not. So this is sent from the forward command post of the 3rd Army, regular combat report, to the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, dated the 14th of August, 1998. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Would you please look at page 2 where there is a report on the previous day, the 13th of August, 1998, and if you see the last line, the last bullet point above, the situation in units of the army, it says: "About 2350 hours a terrorist attack was carried out on members of the police in the village of Bobrdja [phoen], Decani municipality from the direction of the village of Voksa." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And then on page 3 --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have page 3 shown. It's at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Under 5 it says: "I have decided," and in paragraph 2 of point 5 where it says "I have decided," it says: "With Combat Group 15-3 support the MUP forces in routing the DTS strongholds in the areas of the villages of Grabovac, Lodja, Rausic, Voksa." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the needs of the translation the last village was Voksa. It's on page 49, line 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, if you look at the last page, it seems that you as the Chief of Staff signed on behalf of the commander of the 3rd Army, Dusan Samardzic, you signed this combat report?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because the commander was in Pristina, but at that point in time he was not at the forward command post. That's why I signed on his behalf so that the telegram could be sent off, in compliance with the authorities he had given me previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, just a second, please. Just one sentence, please, page 2 of this same document where it says point 3: "The situation in units of the army." It says: "Control and touring of the visits of the Army of Yugoslavia continues on the territory of the -- of Kosovo and Metohija by a team from the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia headed by the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here, and you can see part of the reason why I was the one to sign this because he was touring the units with the Chief of the General Staff or visiting certain structures and organs of government in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So when the decision was made to give support to the MUP units, the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia was in Kosovo and Metohija, he was out on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he was touring the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, could you please look at 5D1175. That's a map and we've scanned it in colour, it's under the same number. I don't know how that can be brought up technically, but we won't waste time on that. General --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see the map and it's quite clear to me. The writing is very tiny, but it's clear. I lived there, I spent a long time in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And in the left upper corner there is the signature of Colonel-General Dusan Samardzic, who approved the execution of this operation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he approved it, not to me, as was interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have Prosecution Exhibit P1428.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, you have before you a decision on breaking up DTS forces in the village of Slup and Voksa dated the 14th of August, 1998, signed by the Chief of Staff Colonel Vladimir Lazarevic. Is this decision in line with all the previous decisions we have commented on, as regards support to MUP forces in breaking up terrorist forces and the order of the superior command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did the Chief of Staff have the right to sign this decision, which follows from the decision of the superior command and the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, let's clarify one thing. This decision did not stem from the decision of the superior command. You are alluding to the army. This is a decision of the corps commander that the army commander approved.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Approved.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. That is quite all right. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps commander, or rather, Chief of Staff, did he have the right to sign -- is that what you asked me? Well, that is up to his commander and his Chief of Staff to the extent to which he authorised him because the commander can authorise in certain situations the chief of his staff to sign certain documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now I would like to draw your attention to one particular sentence from this document if you are in a position to explain it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the last page of this document, paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I see it on the screen now, paragraph 6 is in front of you. It is entitled command and communications. Could you please carefully read the sentence that follows and pay attention to this. "Commanding of combat operations," so not units, "shall be carried out by the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija with a forward command post in Djakovica." Can you give us your comment on this sentence.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I can, but in relation to the previous question, had General Lazarevic signed as Chief of Staff, the document would not have been valid because then it would not be legally founded. He signed it as Chief of Staff and that shows the validity of that document. As for my response to this second question of yours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, there's a problem with the translation there. Could you give us that answer again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, you are probably as tense as I am because of time constraints, but we really have to speak at a slower pace. Please speak at a slower pace because the interpreters have a problem. It's already afternoon --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept what you say, but I'm not tense at all and I'll give you my answer slowly. So let me add on to what I responded in terms of your previous question, you asked me whether the Chief of Staff had the right to sign. He signed it the right way. Had it said in the signature "Commander General Lazarevic," then the document would not have been valid from a legal aspect, and you are all lawyers so I don't have to explain it to you. In relation to the second question, commanding combat activities shall be carried out --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sorry. May I just interrupt you at this point because later on it's not going to be clear. Thank you for the legal explanation, but the point of adducing evidence here is for you to give us military explanations. So my question is: From a military point of view, from the point of view of military doctrine, is this order correct, proper, and in line with the order of the army command and the superior command? That was my question. As for legal matters --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is quite valid but just with a small observation that in the letterhead it should have said "command of the Pristina Corps forward command post."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But that's just a formal problem, right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not going into the legal aspect. You ordered me not to go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you to respond to the second part of my question. I am going to repeat it once again because we were dealing with a different subject. Number 6 says: "Commanding combat activities," so not units, "will be carried out for the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija from the forward command post of the PRK in Djakovica." Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can explain. All units that were engaged in carrying out this task - and we can see here that different structures were engaged - that are in different chains of command from one place. Now, to add on to the answer I've already given when I said that there is a so-called unity of command or from where the commanding officer of a particular unit, each and every one actually commands his own units in his own chain of command, not that one commands all units. However, that is why it is called unity of command. We followed the situation together, we reach agreements, we see how the realisation develops, where the problems are. We harmonize together who is supposed to do what. As for executive orders, every commander conveys to his subordinate units --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, essentially you've explained what it is, but for the purposes of the transcript there is a mistake -- I mean the essence of your answer shows that there is a mistake in the transcript. But page 54, line 18 it says "so-called unity of command," and you said "unity of command,"objedinjeno komandno"?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said "objedinjeno komandno mesto," that is to say a single command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Not single, joint command post. [Interpretation] Your Honour, again -- well, the tape can be heard, the witness said "joint command post, "objedinjeno komandno mesto," also earlier on when he answered my question from the point of view of different command posts, on page 37, line 12, that is where it is interpreted correctly, so it is Joint Command post. If there were to be a different interpretation now -- well, we see what the essence is, but there may be confusion in the transcript due to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I would like to know what the witness means by "Joint Command post."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when explaining command posts, the types that exist in our military theory, I said that there is the so-called Joint Command post --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've got -- just a moment. I understand the categories that you gave us earlier, but in this case where was the Joint Command post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this case the Joint Command post was at the forward command post of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And who were -- who formed the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. I never mentioned this term "Joint Command." I am referring to the following term: Joint Command post, that is an area, a building, a facility, a dug-out, a tent where commanders of different structures of units that are engaged in a certain area - and it's indispensable to have commanders who make decisions on combat activities be in one place, nearby, so that through immediate contacts they could resolve the problems observed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, look, please, at paragraph 6 that you're dealing with, does it mention Joint Command post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It does not mention Joint Command post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chief of Staff, Colonel Lazarevic, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In your view, should the reference have been to Joint Command post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It can, but it need not be either. It is important for the chain of command down to the subordinates is not infringed upon in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, could you now read slowly for us the beginning of paragraph 6, the first two lines of paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is what it says literally: "Commanding combat activities shall be carried out by the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija from the forward command post of the Pristina Corps in Djakovica. Communication should be organised" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, that's enough. Thank you. Now, that seems to indicate a body that will command called the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We soldiers do not understand it that way and that is not the way it was in essence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, we must try to interpret the language that's there, and you have very helpfully read it to us. Are you saying that that language does not simply say that operations will be commanded by the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This means that from a single place we commanders of different structures --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, no. Can you answer my question? Are you saying that that language does not simply say that operations will be commanded by the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is what I assert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You wish to tell us that's not what it says? I mean, you may wish to say that's not what it means, I understand that; but are you telling us that the simple language there is not that operations are to be commanded by the Joint Command? And if you're saying that, would you read it again just to be absolutely sure that there is no mistake in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness did confirm that that is what is written there. The witness confirmed that. He read it out to you, and that is absolutely what is written there, but he tried to explain. Perhaps there is a mistake in the interpretation and there is a lack of understanding, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, let me complete this part of the questioning. If you look at line 14, you'll see I asked him whether the language doesn't simply say what he's already read to us, and he says that that's what he asserts, it doesn't say that. And I'm asking him just to be absolutely clear about it that he's saying that this language doesn't say what he read to us. That's what he -- that's what you're actually claiming, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not claim that that is not written there. I read it out as written, but in my further explanation I said that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Simic, you did say that and that's one thing. But I entirely understand that you may wish to tell us it doesn't mean what it says, and that's the explanation you wish to give us. And I think you've already given that explanation. And I just wanted to be clear that no one here is in any doubt about what that passage actually says. Let's proceed, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, we talked at length, and in this case for one year now this has been discussed. If you know and if you can give me an answer, answer this question; but if not, never mind. A simple question: What is referred to here is that there was a Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija that infringed upon the chain of command. My question is: Had there been a Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija, would it be necessary for the Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia in April 1999 make an order to resubordinate the MUP to the army, would there have been a need for that had there been a Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was an order made to resubordinate the MUP to the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, an order was made by the president on the resubordination of MUP units to the Army of Yugoslavia, on the basis of which General Ojdanic issued his order. I cannot quote the date for you, but I think it was the second half of April when -- well, please don't take my word for it. It is approximately the 18th of April, if I remember correctly, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that order complied with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, do you know why this order was not complied with?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of an obstruction on the part of the highest-ranking control, or rather, command organs in Serbia's MUP and not just in Serbia's MUP, I apologise, also in Montenegro's MUP because Yugoslavia still existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Therefore you will agree with me that this was not fictitious order. This was not something that was feigned to suit a different goal, a different purpose; that was in all honesty an order to attempt to carry out resubordination?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was by no means a fictitious order.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Now that we're at it, I do have one last question about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please call up 3D692, item 11, I believe the page number is 4. Can we have a look, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'll be asking you to read the first sentence of the first paragraph of item 11. The report is dated the 29th of May, 1999, item 11, please. You have it in B/C/S. Would you please be so kind, first paragraph, first sentence, read it out for us.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although I did not see the first pages of this document, I do recognise it. This is a report in which I was involved. Item 11 reads: "In the area of responsibility there is no singleness of command over all units, but rather relations with the units of the MUP are implemented by agreement which very often, especially at lower levels, is not something that is complied."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, sir, does this of all things not prove exactly what we have been talking about?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: There was no Joint Command, in other words, right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't answer that question. That's a matter for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, sir, I only have two or three questions for you and they are about the control that you conducted between the 23rd and the 26th of May 1999, at the Pristina Corps command. What was your assessment of the functioning of the Pristina Corps and among the subordinate units, who commanded the corps and the brigades?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained this extensively yesterday about this particular inspection or control. We ascertained that work was organised at the corps level, that combat documents were detailed, and that any orders received were being carried out in keeping with the original orders that were received and in keeping with certain problems and situations. And we also found a couple of weaknesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, sir, thank you very much for your answers and for your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, General Simic, sir. My name is Dan Ivetic and I will have only a few questions for you so you can relax they will only be four to five questions so we will go quickly through them. Now, first of all -- and they're going to be specifically related to your statement, but I'd like to since we have the document up on the screen, this 3D692 that my learned colleague, Mr. Bakrac, just asked you to read paragraph 11 of. I'd like to ask you if you have any knowledge that the staff of the high command ever in written form advised Minister of the Interior, Vlajko Stojiljkovic, of the matters set forth in paragraph 11 of this document; and if so, when and where that document can be found?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is a very simple one. Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command, in this case General Ojdanic, is not superior to the minister of the interior and he was in no position to send him that order. In that case, he would have commanded him. The order should have come from whoever was the minister of the interior's superior, which in this case was the president or the prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, just to be clear, I'm talking about not any order, I'm talking about this -- the matters set forth in 11 of this document that's in front of you, 3D692, the report from April - I don't have the English up in front of me to be able to go to the first page quickly - from April the 20 -- or May the 29th, 1999, the staff of the high command -- of the Supreme Command. Was that information ever communicated to Minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic by the chief of the supreme -- Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're asking me to give you an answer that I'm not best placed to provide. If you go through this entire document, in addition to all the weaknesses that we noted we ordered the subordinates to deal with these weaknesses. Likewise, we made proposals to General Ojdanic to take certain measures through his own superior, and that was the state president, for him to deal with this problem to resolve it. This is explicitly stated in our reports, among other things, but we couldn't order General Ojdanic to do that for the president for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay, sir, and again I apologise for pausing, although I can understand you in Serbian, I have to wait for the transcript to catch up with us so we don't have a problem for the translators. Now I'd like to move to your written statement, it's going to be 3D1089, although I don't believe it will be necessary --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But if the witness does need to refer to it perhaps it should be on -- ready in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General, sir, I just want like to ask you about two particular portions of your statement, first I'd like to focus on paragraph 24 of the same wherein you state that: "At the level of the staff of the Supreme Command as well as the General Staff there existed no plan for ethnic cleansing in Kosovo-Metohija as regards that organ." Now, am I correct that you as a member of the General Staff, and later the staff of the Supreme Command, did not have any evidence proving that such a plan existed with respect to any organ of the FRY or the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I must be very circumspect in my answer because I find the question to be less specific than desirable. In paragraph 24 I'm talking about the General Staff of the VJ, and you're asking me about the other organs as well. I assert and I guarantee, because I spent ten years working on wartime planning, that no such plan ever existed. Nowhere at no time was anything like this ever discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that bit, General, but I asked you a different question. As a member of the General Staff of the VJ and as a member of the Supreme Command, is it true that you never had any files, any knowledge, that any other organ of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or the Republic of Serbia had any plan whatsoever, a plan like this, against the Albanians in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [In English] For the sake of clarity I'll have to revert back to English since my questions are phrased that way. Now, General, I'd like to direct your attention to paragraph 19 of your statement which you've already started to discuss here where you state that: "An order was issued for units of the MUP on the territory of Kosovo-Metohija to be resubordinated to the command of the Pristina Corps," and you indicated just prior to my questions that this was -- that this order was issued by the president of Yugoslavia. The question I have for you is: Did you personally have occasion to see any such written order issued by the president of Yugoslavia regarding resubordination of the MUP in this manner?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know where such a document could be located?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such a document is in the archives of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Do you have personal knowledge of the fact that such a document was ever forwarded to Minister of the Interior, Vlajko Stojiljkovic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, you're asking me a question that I cannot answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you don't know, please state so.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that I don't know, but it's not within the competence of General Ojdanic, the Chief of the General Staff, to issue that order to a -- to an organ of the federal government. That's what I'm talking about. I believe we're talking at cross-purposes. It is within his competence to command the army on behalf of the president and not to issue orders to bodies or organs of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [In English] Can we take -- sorry, I had to wait for the transcript. Can we take it from your answer then that there was never any written order or directive issued by the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command and addressed to the Minister of the Interior, Vlajko Stojiljkovic regarding resubordination of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can't assert this with 100 per cent certainty, but knowing General Ojdanic I know that he would never exceed his authority because he never did. There would be no foundation for him to give orders to the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The last question I have for you, sir, is: Do you have knowledge of any written response or decree received by the staff of the high command of the army -- the Supreme Command, excuse me, from Minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic of the MUP refusing to implement resubordination?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this is linked to the previous answer. I never saw a document like that from the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia at the Supreme Command Staff in terms of them refusing to subordinate themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Question and that is all the questions I have for you --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But we do have a written document from the Ministry of the Interior of Montenegro --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That much I know and we've had that discussed -- I've already asked questions about that and I don't wish to take up more court time on that, General. I wanted to save you some additional questioning. Thank you for your answers, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further cross-examination for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. [Trial Chamber and legal officer confer].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It might be best if we were to break now, Mr. Hannis, and then you would have an uninterrupted run to the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That would be great, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, we will break for 20 minutes now. If you could again please leave the courtroom with the usher, and we will resume as close as we can to ten minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, you will now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, I don't know what the practice is in court but I wish to present a request to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, what is your request?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In connection with the question of General Lukic's counsel why the MUP was not resubordinated, I explicitly answered because of obstruction by high-ranking leading people. As I don't have any knowledge as to whether they received such an order or not, may I withdraw this statement of mine and instead have my answer recorded as: I don't know. Because I don't wish to speculate and it's not in line with my solemn declaration, and I truly don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, we note what you say, but we'll not be deleting anything from the record, the evidence. We'll look at everything that has been said in due course and draw appropriate conclusions on all the evidence that we have heard in the case. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I'm going to start out by sort of going in the order of questions that were asked you first by Mr. Visnjic and then by the other Defence counsel. And I will start when you were working at the Supreme Command Staff in April of 1999. Mr. Visnjic showed you a couple of documents that are -- appear to be briefing notes from those evening meetings you had at the Supreme Command Staff. Do you recall those? I just have a general --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have a general question about how those were taken. Do you know who took those notes of the briefings?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those briefings were held in the hall of the operations centre, and there were persons on duty in that operations centre and they did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the practice, were the notes that were taken then later circulated to you all to review and make any corrections or did you -- did you ever see them?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Minutes were taken at the meeting or, conditionally speaking, collegium because there were the members of the collegium of the Chief of Staff, General Ojdanic, there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I think we're talking about two different things now. I'm aware of the collegium meetings which I understand were tape recorded, and often those meetings seemed to last for hours and the documents run to 40 or 50 pages. But now I'm talking about during the war and these sort of end-of-the-day briefings around 7.00 or 8.00 at night, that was something different, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But the collegium minutes composition, it was like a collegium. So that's what determines whether it's a collegium, who was there not how long it lasted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But these meetings in the evening were not called collegium meetings, were they, even though you all are part of the collegium?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, they were called daily briefings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And the minutes or the notes that were taken of those daily meetings, were they tape recorded or were they simply written down by someone?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Minutes were taken by persons from the operations administration in whose competence the operative centre was, they were in charge of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So they were not tape recorded as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be explicit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And did you ever see the notes that were taken at these meetings, were they ever passed around to you or other members to review and make corrections?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Based on these minutes or these notes, we looked at the tasks that had been set and each participant, if he had not had time to note something down during the meeting or found something unclear, he could look at those minutes and extract what he needed from the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And were the ones -- were the notes that were circulated to you all after the meetings, were they typed up or were they just simply xeroxed copies of the handwritten notes?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These notes were not distributed to us. They were kept in the operations centre in a certain place, and anyone who was interested could go and inspect the entire record.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You told us about the big map --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move from that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we just look very quickly at 3D724. Thank you very much. Yes. That can go from the screen. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, can we leave it there while it's up. I'll ask a question about that one. I'll skip ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, if we could go -- I guess it is page 3 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S, it's item number 12 I have a question about. In your testimony yesterday you mentioned the Vinca Institute and you told us it's a well-known nuclear institute and there's a lot of radioactive matter being stored there. What exactly was the Vinca Institute?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Vinca institute, as you yourself have said, was a nuclear institute where nuclear research was carried out with nuclear material, radioactive material, dangerous to the environment and to humans.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in item number 12 of Exhibit 3D724, Major-General Petkovic is noted as speaking and he mentions it's possible the Vinca Institute may be damaged and it's thought that a nuclear bomb cannot be created. Were there discussions or plans at that time to create a nuclear bomb at the Vinca Institute?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, in the leadership of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia there was never any idea of creating a nuclear bomb. The Vinca Institute did scientific research.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know why Major-General would then feel it necessary to make that comment?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say why he said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want to return -- I started to ask you a question about the map. You mentioned this large map about I think 1 and a half by 1 and a half metres that at one time you were tasked to help make some markings on. How did this work, was the map changed every day to reflect changes on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The map was not changed every day, but rather, as I said yesterday, various subcolours were used to mark the activities of individual units in the course of the day. General Ojdanic, in view of the fact that it was quite small and then became very hard to read over time, ordered that we should find a better method of keeping that map.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And did you find a better method?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After the first attempt to which General Ojdanic had some comments to make, we developed the method and I explained what we did yesterday, how we solved the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You have to be patient with me. I'm trying to visualise what this looked like. Is this a topographic map of Kosovo or is this all of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As it was war, the entire territory of the FRY was called the theatre of war by our soldiers. It was a map of the FRY with all the units where they were deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is this a paper map or is there a plastic cover or a plate of glass over it? How do you -- how were you marking on the map?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning it had a plastic cover and felt-tip pens were used, following the methods in the instructions for work were made on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And so at the end of each day then it got erased and changed to show the new locations of units, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. By your leave, if -- to vulgarize it. There was a unit in a certain area, and on that day they had no activities, it remained that way. If it did engage in some activity, then this would be shown with a felt-tip pen with a subcolour, and in the legend the date would be entered when the change was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But were those changes then stored somehow, did you take a photograph of the map at the end of each day to show how things had progressed from day one to day 50, for example?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no photograph was made of the map. It was always on the wall in the operations centre, and apart from what I've already said that certain subcolours were used and marked with a date in the legend, changes were also introduced in the war diary, they were entered in the war diary. And after a certain period of time had elapsed, a prolonged period of time, the map would become difficult to read, it would be saturated. And then on that day a new map would be introduced with the situation as of that day, and then the markings would continue to be made on this second map and the first map would be registered and kept in the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. That -- thank you. That's very helpful. So you marked on the map until it got to the point that it was so covered with markings that you needed to start over with a new map, correct, and --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, not a new, clean map. The initial map would reflect the day on which it starts. So it would not be a clean map, it would have on it the situation as it was on that day. The old map would still be in the operations centre, but it would simply be kept as a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And that -- those maps that you used during the war should still be available in the VJ archives, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. What was the smallest level unit that was shown on those maps -- I see you're indicating your headphones there. Are you not hearing me?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I didn't hear you before, but now I hear. According to our rules, the working map is always kept for two degrees below, which means that as it was the Supreme Command Staff, apart from the army zone and the zone of the corps, it would be up to corps level because of the specific circumstances in which combat activities were carried out in Kosovo, brigades were also entered but with only one line and the number would be shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So not battalions, but brigades would be shown on the map in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What about -- was there anything to indicate MUP units because they were engaged in combat operations with the Pristina Corps, or was it only VJ units that were shown on the map?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only VJ units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And military territorial detachments, are they too small to be reflected on the map?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military territorial detachments were part of the command of the army, they were subordinated to the command of the army. But the Pristina Military District was then subordinate -- or resubordinated, excuse me, to the commander of the Pristina Corps because of their specific nature, and they are shown in the areas where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What about civil defence?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Units of the civil defence did not come within the purview of the Chief of Staff, and they are not shown but they were entered in the war diary from the combat reports, as reported by the subordinate commander. And from that you can see where they were and what they were doing. That's only for purposes of monitoring or following, not for purposes of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And would the same be true for MUP units that were engaged in operations, would they be reflected in the -- in the war diary?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if -- if they were mentioned in the report submitted by the subordinate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. In one of those briefing notes Mr. Visnjic asked you about a reference to training of volunteers, I think it was 126 volunteers; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't recall the precise number, but I accept what you say, yes. Not just 126, there was a cycle of training. When I referred to General Ojdanic, I said that that cycle had been completed and that as far as I can recall those 126 had been sent on to the subordinate command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, were those volunteers taken in as a unit or are you talking about 126 different individuals that went different places, if you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a centre for the training of volunteers in Bubanj Potok. There they were trained to individually carry out their tasks. General Ojdanic issued an order that the volunteers should be distributed among the subordinate units and that they should not make up a separate unit by themselves, but that according to their military specialty they should fill the empty places, the vacancies, in various units depending on what they were specially trained to do. So they were not a special volunteer unit. That was ordered by him explicitly, he prohibited the creation of such a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that is right. One of the reasons for that, sir, is that the VJ and the JNA before it had had some bad experience with volunteer units; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to answer that question because you asked me about the Army of Yugoslavia. If you meant that members of the Army of Yugoslavia as those who inherited the JNA and continued it, then yes; if you're asking me as the Army of Yugoslavia, the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And is it your testimony that there was no problem for the VJ with volunteers in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general, yes; individually, no -- no, no, generally no; individually, yes. Excuse me, I made an error.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think I understand. Now, I want to ask you about Exhibit 3D725.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 5 of the English and page 5 of the B/C/S at the very last bit of text on that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, this is -- these are the briefing notes for a meeting on the 8th of April, 1999, and if you could look at the next-to-the-last bullet point on your page. And I can tell you that from the previous page this appears to be General Ojdanic speaking, and that next-to-the-last item says: "The position on volunteers, resolve it. The patriot must be given the opportunity of going into battle rather than looters of various types." Do you recall that being discussed at that meeting on your first week at the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've partially answered that in my previous answer. There was a brief order issued by General Ojdanic as to how volunteers were to be dealt with, how they were to be received, how they were to be trained, what was to be done with them apart from the medical and psychological processing, monitoring the training after a certain period of training, according to the assessment of the officers carrying out the training --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, all you were asked was do you recall this being discussed at that particular meeting, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General -- so it looks like on April 8th the issue of volunteers is still not resolved because General Ojdanic is saying: Resolve it, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By your leave, there is a letter from the command of the 3rd Army where he draws attention to problems with the volunteers, but as I can't make a link between this date and that document, I assume that General Ojdanic had in mind that when receiving, processing, and training volunteers, evidently some mistakes had been made which were now showing up in practice in the way he explained here. He said looters of various types and so on. I assume that that's what this refers to, but it's hard to make the link because I don't know when that letter from the command of the 3rd Army arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Next I want to ask you about Exhibit P929. These are the minutes of a VJ collegium meeting on the 9th of April, 1999. Mr. Visnjic asked you about this I think at page 15482. And I think you told us you recalled this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 13 of the English, and I believe that is the bottom of page 13 and the top of page 14 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall speaking at that meeting and talking about the ground forces in Kosovo and their situation and what they had been doing?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And so during the first two weeks or two weeks and a couple of days of the war, the ground forces in Kosovo, the forces of the 3rd Army, the Pristina Corps, you say these units have been engaged on protecting the state border, crushing the Siptar terrorist forces, and closing the routes which lead from Macedonia and Albania, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the course of crushing the Siptar terrorist forces, isn't it correct that the VJ in coordination with the MUP in those operations were also driving out the Kosovar Albanian civilians who lived in those areas where the Siptar terrorists were operating?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, what was happening with those civilians who lived in those areas where those combat operations were carried out in the first two weeks of the war?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have partly given an answer to that question. It's natural where combat operations are being carried out and people are being killed that the population from such areas tries to take shelter, tries to flee, that's one reason. A second reason is that the terrorist army of Kosovo, in order to achieve their propaganda goals and stage humanitarian disaster, exerted pressure on their compatriots to move out of their villages, on the one hand to achieve their propaganda goal and on the other hand to have a clear field in order to facilitate the air-strikes by the aggressor on the units of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There weren't any combat operations in Pristina town itself, were there, in the first two weeks?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mean yes there were not?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just one thing, please. I came, I came on the 2nd of April to the staff of the Supreme Command. Prior to that for two months, or rather, three months I had been involved in other issues at the defence ministry. So please, if possible, can you keep the questions restricted to the time during which I was responsible to the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand about your change in positions, but I'm just asking if even though you were not working at the Supreme Command Staff, do you have any information that there were combat operations in Pristina town in the first two weeks of the war?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And are you -- are you aware that there were thousands of Kosovo Albanians who were taken to the train station and taken out of the country or taken to the last train stop in Kosovo where they were ordered off the train and marched across the railroad tracks into Macedonia, were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In one of your answers to Mr. Visnjic about the situation of the ground forces on April 8th, 1999, at page 15842, line 24, you said one of the things you were trying to do was "to build fortifications, to reinforce, to try to improve on some of our weaknesses in terms of discipline and such-like." What specifically were you referring to when you said "weaknesses in terms of discipline and such-like"?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that you've been following my testimony about the controls, and it's all there for everyone to see. We established that certain units had not built the shelters and fortifications that could have protected them from air-strikes. That's one thing. And the other thing is they were not complying with camouflage discipline which was exposing our positions, leaving them open. Thirdly, there were random cases of drunkenness and desertion, and such-like, unauthorised entry into villages and such-like. It was in that context that I said it that we had sufficient time and there was to be no ground attack. And we had sufficient time to deal with this, to repair this, and to reinforce our positions for soldiers to be able to hide under the ground, if you like, in order to avoid unnecessary casualties as a result of air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And also in that April 9th meeting you talked about that there was a concern that there was going to be a NATO ground operation; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that at the Supreme Command Staff there was always the concern that sooner or later there would be is a ground operation, and I also explained about the two different possible scenarios.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Right. And you did mention those two scenarios, one with a large group of the terrorist army in Kosovo with support from the Albanian army, and I think the second one was if NATO itself brought in some of its soldiers to set up a bridge head [Realtime transcript read in error "hit"]. Those were the two options. Okay --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were both of those options something that you and the VJ expected from the very start of the war? I know you didn't come to the Supreme Command Staff until April 3rd, but do you know if that was something that was anticipated from day one of the war?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you remember, I spoke yesterday about the initial operations planned and how the directive was produced which was a consequence of this collegium meeting. This was a directive on Thunder 3, Grom 3, and this was elaborated by the General Staff on the 16th of January. This directive comprised the possibility that the aggression would start by the bringing in of a multi-national NATO brigade from the north of Macedonia, partly air-borne, by helicopter and partly across the line through the Kacanicka ravine and in cooperation with the forces in Kosovo in order to create this bridge head, as you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 80, line 14, says bridge hit and what Mr. Hannis asked was bridge head and I think there's enough difference there that it might not be caught and it's an important difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: While we're on this issue I want to ask you about the Supreme Command. You were part of the Supreme Command Staff. What was your understanding about who made up the Supreme Command during the state of war?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, would you agree with me that everyone understood that Slobodan Milosevic was the supreme commander during the state of war?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And my understanding is that the VJ General Staff, as it was called during peacetime, once the state of war declared became the Supreme Command Staff, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, in my language in English if I were talking about a Supreme Command Staff, I would understand that to be the staff, the people, that worked for the Supreme Command, whoever or whatever that was. My question is: What was the Supreme Command? Who was the Supreme Command? Was it only Mr. Milosevic or was it some larger group of persons, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do know. How wouldn't I? Each command has a structure and so does the Supreme Command. At the head you find the commander, and then there is a staff which analyses, or rather, transforms orders of the commander in a technical sense into a certain document and then sends this document down to those subordinated to him to carry out in the simplest of terms. Therefore, if you ask me whether the president, too, was part of the Supreme Command, in that case the answer is a categorical yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But is he the only one in the Supreme Command or are there other persons along with Mr. Milosevic who are part of the Supreme Command which is served by the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Supreme Command Staff works for the commanders alone. If I understand this correctly and if I may I suppose you're allusion to is to the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to. I was just having a comment on the transcript and the witness has says the Supreme Command Staff works for the commander alone, for the commander alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Commander --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You heard that, General. Was that your answer, that the Supreme Command Staff works for the commander alone, was that your answer?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that means just Slobodan Milosevic because he's the commander, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I don't understand your question. It doesn't work for him; it works for the VJ. It does for the VJ what he orders to his Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The Supreme Command Staff doesn't work for Mr. Milosevic as supreme commander, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. It wouldn't be right. If I were Chief of Staff, as I was, and I would not be working for my army commander. That is the same kind of relationship. The staff is in charge of all combat documents in the spirit of the commander's decision. The same principle applies at all levels, including that of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me try to approach this from a different direction. You mentioned the Supreme Defence Council. What was your understanding about what that was and who was on it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Supreme Defence Council comprises president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the president of the Republic of Serbia, and the president of the Republic of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is based on their decisions that the supreme commander over the army grows out of this body and the Supreme Defence Council in a more liberal sense deals with the country's defence, because the armed struggle waged by the army is the basic implementing agent of the country's defence. But it's not the only subject of defence, there are other subjects of defence. So the Supreme Defence Council deals with all the subjects of the country's defence because the means to wage this struggle is the economy, traffic, agriculture, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's -- we've had evidence in this case and it's been my understanding that during peacetime the Supreme Defence Council, which as you said was made up of the president of the Republic of Yugoslavia, Mr. Milosevic; the president of the Republic of Serbia, who we know was Mr. Milutinovic; and the president of Montenegro, who we know at that time was Mr. Djukanovic, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it's my understanding that according to the constitution of Yugoslavia and the Law on Defence and the Law on the Army all provide that the Supreme Defence Council -- that the president of the Republic of Yugoslavia commands the army during peacetime in accordance with decisions of the Supreme Defence Council; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What happens to the Supreme Defence Council when a state of war is declared?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a while ago from the aspect of the country's defence which subjects were involved in this defence. It wasn't just the army. The supreme commander exercises command over the army, and then through reporting every morning of the supreme commander the same information that the supreme commander had was also received by the next member of the Supreme Defence Council. And it was based on this that they could survey the problems in the army from their own standpoints, the standpoint of the economy, the railways, traffic in general, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My understanding of your answer to be then that Mr. Milutinovic and Mr. Djukanovic continued to serve, but they only dealt with problems like the economy and the railway and traffic and nothing to do with the army; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no -- maybe I misunderstood. Maybe it was misinterpreted. I allow for both possibilities. Maybe I misexpressed myself. The Supreme Defence Council, when it took the decision for the army to engage in the country's defence, and that was when the government declared a state of war, President Milosevic commands the army and this doesn't mean that the remaining members of the Supreme Defence Council are entirely passive. He commands with their conveyed decisions, the decisions that they took or agreed on, but the report sent by the chief of the Supreme Command Staff to his own commander also are submitted to the members of the Supreme Defence Council, but also to the president of the federal government, the president of the Republic of Serbia, and let me not get into any further into that. I think there are 15 or 16 addresses that this report is submitted to and then they use this to see what their duties and responsibilities are from the point of view of the functional duty that the army and other subjects of defence must carry out. My apologies, if I may. We, for example, if you looked at the report you know that they were saying they were short on certain types of ammunition or this or that or maybe this. There is no industry because it's a special-purpose industry because it's destroyed, so this had to be important this can't be done by the army or by the Chief of Staff. This must be done by one of the federal bodies. It was in this sense that they had a commitment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we've heard some evidence to suggest that once the state of war was declared the Supreme Defence Council did not meet during the war, but we've heard people refer to the Supreme Command. Now, my question to you: Is the body that's referred to as the Supreme Command during the state of war what used to be called the Supreme Defence Council during peacetime and they just changed the name because you're in a different state when the war is on.?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's one thing I'd like to ask you and it's this. In my opinion the Supreme Defence Council once it transfers its powers under the constitution to the president and he becomes the supreme commander, they are not within the composition of the Supreme Command in order to exercise direct command over the army, because this would disrupt the fundamental elementary principle of subordination and singleness of command. You can't have the one, the other, and somebody else on top of that issuing orders to the army. It was in this sense that the principle of singleness of command was complied with and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But wouldn't it be possible for the supreme commander to have advisors or associates that he consulted with in taking the decisions about how to employ the army?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to object. The question's been asked at least three different ways and answered each way the same -- in the same manner by the witness. And this last question now is just asking for speculation based on a very concrete and direct answers given by the witness to these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have to say speaking for myself, Mr. O'Sullivan, I don't understand the last answer. And I -- once Mr. Hannis is finished, I'll certainly be exploring this further myself on behalf of the Chamber. It's -- these answers are not clear. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me move to something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please do not invite the witness to engage in speculation, but the last question probably didn't do that, however you're departing from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm going to stick to the topic but I'm going to move to another question. Could we go to this P929, the exhibit that we've got. I need to move to page 38 and 39 of the English and I think that is page 45 in the B/C/S, yeah, 45 carrying over to 46.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I don't know if you can see that on your screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I need to start at the bottom, the last -- I think the last six lines on that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me read in the English and then you tell me if this is what it says in the B/C/S, and I'm starting on page 38 of the English five lines up from the bottom. This is General Ojdanic speaking and he says: "I mentioned that a conclusion should be given which will confirm how that will affect the possibility of continuing the arm struggle, particularly from the perspective of time. To conduct an armed struggle in conditions of the predicted further course of the war. As for me, as early as tomorrow I will ask the Supreme Command to thoroughly acquaint itself with this material, regardless of how extensive it is and I think that it will not be very extensive." And at some point in time we're going to have to turn the page in both English and B/C/S. "I will suggest that after that in a group determined by the Supreme Command, the president, briefed that group to a lesser extent on the stands, assessments, conclusions and proposals of the staff of the Supreme Command as regards what should be done at this time." Did I read it correctly? Is that translation correct? Is there anything in the B/C/S that is different?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite frankly, I was not able to follow in the Serbian. I didn't have the portion that you were reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, could we go back one page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General, if you could start reading -- actually, I have a hard copy and maybe if I could have the usher hand you this. I've highlighted part of it in pink here. If you could start from that first little half circle of the pink and read until you run out of pink.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you read from that part.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "As for me, as early as tomorrow I will ask the Supreme Command, regardless of their extent and I don't think they will be very extensive to thoroughly familiarise themselves with it. I will also propose that based on this in the composition determined by the supreme commander, to a lesser degree, the president, familiarises this composition with the positions."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and then the next page. "Familiarises this composition with the positions, assessments, conclusions and proposals of the staff of the Supreme Command as to what needs doing right now at this time."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I think we should have read again the sentence: "I will also propose that ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mean before "as for me"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, the next sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: "I will suggest that ..." -- Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Mr. Simic, will you read again the sentence that begins: "I will also propose that based on this in the composition ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it reads literally: "As for me, as early as tomorrow I will ask the Supreme Command, regardless of their extent and I don't think they will be very extensive, to thoroughly familiarise themselves with these documents. I will also propose that after this in a composition determined by the supreme commander, to a lesser degree, the president, familiarises this composition with the positions, assessments, conclusions, and proposals made by the Supreme Command Staff as to what needs doing or what must be done right now at this time."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In the first sentence you read there you read the words "Supreme Command." And in the second sentence you read the words "Supreme commander." Are these -- are the words in these two sentences different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says: "I will ask the Supreme Command to familiarise themselves with this material." And it also makes a reference in the last sentence to the supreme commander, the president, to a lesser degree familiarise the composition with the positions," so both terms are used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did I clear it up for you, Your Honour, I'm not sure it cleared it up for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It doesn't clear it. It has confirmed that the witness read two different terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Um --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And he says that there are different terms in the Serb --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I wonder, Your Honour, if we can inquire of the booth if we can have the document on the screen for them. I think it's an important point to clear up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it's a very important point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The trouble is we have to start on the previous page and continue over to the second page, but I think it would be worth the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we not just put the copy that the witness has on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that could be read -- the highlighted portion could be read to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
